S A T A N I C

Responsive Web Design

With consumers using so many varied devices to access the internet these days, it is increasingly troublesome to create "static" designs. The solution to this problem is a concept known as "Responsive Web Design".

Wikipedia describes Responsive Web Design like this:

Responsive web design (RWD) is an approach to web design aimed at crafting sites to provide an optimal viewing and interaction experience—easy reading and navigation with a minimum of resizing, panning, and scrolling—across a wide range of devices (from desktop computer monitors to mobile phones).

I hope to help you all achieve a small glimpse at the utility of this design concept. For this guide, we will be creating a responsive header image. That is, a header image that will always scale to 100% width, no matter the screen resolution, while still maintaining aspect ratio (no weird "stretching"), and without creating any ugly white spaces (or gaps) in the page.

The Problem

So you have this awesome banner image that you want to use for your header image, you spend a while resizing it to get things looking just right, and it does!... until you check it out on your phone and half of the image is cut off! But wait, maybe you thought of that possibility and made sure to tell the image to be 100% wide... but then you have to set a static height which great on your monitor!... but creates a small gap on your friend's monitor and a huge gap on your phone.

What You Wanted

Responsive Header Image

You can see the whole header image in both desktop and mobile browsers, and anything in-between.

Keep reading to see how!

Image Gets Cut Off

Correct Height, Image Gets Cut Off

#header{ 
 background: url('https://veuwer.com/i/2v8b.png') no-repeat;
 height: 400px;
}

100% Wide With Gaps

Whole Image, Huge Gap

#header{ 
 background: url('https://veuwer.com/i/2v8b.png') no-repeat;
 background-size: 100%;
 height: 400px;
}

Responsive Header Image

Let's get right into it, here is the CSS template that you will be using:

#header{ 
 background: url('backgroundimage.ext') no-repeat;
 background-size: contain;
 background-position: 0 sr_header_area_px;
 width: 100%;
 height: 0;
 padding-bottom: calc(image_aspect_ratio_% + sr_header_area_px + header_container_px);
}
@media (max-width: 950px){
 #header{ 
 background-position: 0 sr_header_area_sm_px;
 padding-bottom: calc(image_aspect_ratio_% + sr_header_area_sm_px + header_container_px);
 }
}

Whoa! That looks complicated!

I know, I know, but work through it with me, just this once, and you'll see that there's nothing to be intimidated by here, I promise!

Making It Your Own

As you can see above, there are a couple of variables that you'll need to fill in, based on your own background image.

backgroundimage.ext: Pretty straightforward, fill in the URL of your background image.

sr_header_area_px: This is the height of your #sr-header-area element, by default it is 22px.

image_aspect_ratio_%: To calculate this the dimensions of your background image and the following formula: (height/width)*100 (Round this to the nearest two decimal places.)

header_container_px: This is the height of your #header-container element, by default it is 58px.

sr_header_area_sm_px: This is the height of your #sr-header-area element, when the browser windows is 950px or smaller (tablets, phones, etc), by default it is 18px.

Example

Making It My Own

Here I will fill out the template using an example background image.

backgroundimage.ext: https://veuwer.com/i/2v8b.png (1920w x 400h)

sr_header_area_px: I haven't changed my #sr-header-area size, so I'll leave this at 22px

image_aspect_ratio_%: (400/1920)*100 = 20.833333333, we round this to 20.83%

header_container_px: I haven't changed my #header-container size, so I'll leave this at 58px

sr_header_area_sm_px: I haven't changed my #sr-header-area size for mobile devices, so I'll leave this at 18px

The Finished CSS

#header{ 
 background: url('https://veuwer.com/i/2v8b.png') no-repeat;
 background-size: contain;
 background-position: 0 22px;
 width: 100%;
 height: 0;
 padding-bottom: calc(20.83% + 22px + 58px);
}
@media (max-width: 950px){
 #header{ 
 background-position: 0 18px;
 padding-bottom: calc(20.83% + 18px + 58px);
 }
}

Considerations

Simplified version

If you don't particularly care about the top 4px of your image, and your image is not both very wide and very short, you can use a simplified version of the code, like this:

#header{ 
 background: url('backgroundimage.ext') no-repeat;
 background-size: contain;
 background-position: 0 sr_header_area_sm_px;
 width: 100%;
 height: 0;
 padding-bottom: calc(image_aspect_ratio_% + sr_header_area_sm_px + header_container_px);
}

By using the sr_header_area_sm_px value (default 18px) regardless of screen size, you can leave out the whole @media section. Keep in mind that when on a desktop display, you will lose the top 4px of your background image. If you have a very wide and very short image (Ex: 1920px*80px), this will cause part of your image to be covered up on mobile devices and small browser windows.

Extremely low image_aspect_ratio_%

If you have a very long and very short image (Ex: 1920px*80px), you will end up with a very low image_aspect_ratio_%. If the value of your image_aspect_ratio_% is too low, around 5%, you might find part of your header image gets covered on mobile devices or smaller browser windows. To prevent this, you may have to add a little extra to your image_aspect_ratio_% value in the @media (max-width: 950px){...} section. I have found that simply adding 1% seems to correct the issue caused by doing math with such small numbers.

In the example of an image that was 1920px*80px, you would calculate an image_aspect_ratio_% of 4.17%. You would therefore want to use 4.17% in the top half of your code, and 5.17% in the @media (max-width: 950px){...} section.

Combining sr_header_area_px and header_container_px

If you are so inclined, yes, you can do the simple addition math for sr_header_area_px and header_container_px yourself in the padding-bottom: equation. In my example, I could have used padding-bottom: calc(20.83% + 80px); instead.

Common Issues with padding-bottom

If you have problems getting the padding to work, please make sure that there is a space between any + symbols, and that your sr_header_area_px and header_container_px end with px.

Transparent or hidden #sr-header-area

If you have a transparent #sr-header-area, or you have #sr-header-area hidden, you'll notice that the background does not actually start until 22px down the screen. In this case, you'll want to omit the background-position: so that your background image starts at the very top. Make sure to omit the sr_header_area_px addition from the padding-bottom: equation as well.

Conclusion

I hope that this guide has been informative and easy to follow. I also hope that this taste of Responsive Web Design will spur you into looking for more ways to implement Responsive Web Design when customizing your subverses! If more people come together and adopt this design philosophy, it will make for a much more enjoyable browsing experience as our audiences increasingly access our content from more and more varied devices.

Thank you for taking the time to read through and consider this guide, I hope it finds you well.

Cheers!
